text: You've now seen the Application CRD, Flux's Source and Kustomization pieces, and the repo layouts they point at. This lesson puts all of it to work in one concrete sequence: how a single change actually travels from a developer's pull request to running safely in production.

One rule holds the whole workflow together: promote the artifact, don't rebuild it. The exact same container image, identified by an immutable tag or digest, moves unchanged through dev, staging, and prod — only the Git-tracked config saying which overlay points at which tag ever changes. Rebuilding per environment reopens the exact bug class GitOps exists to close: a different cached layer or a dependency that resolved differently means staging's green test run no longer proves anything about what prod will actually run.

It starts with one build. A merge to main triggers CI to build the image once, tag it with a Git SHA or release version, and push it. A bot then opens a PR bumping that same tag into the dev overlay's kustomization file. That PR merges, and ArgoCD or Flux reconciles it into dev within minutes, where automated smoke tests confirm the build actually works.

Promotion itself is just a PR whose diff is often a single line: the identical tag, copied from dev's overlay into staging's, nothing rebuilt and nothing re-tagged. After staging validation — more automated tests, sometimes a manual QA sign-off — a second promotion PR copies that same tag into the prod overlay, usually gated by required reviewers since this is the change customers will actually see.

Watch health status, not just sync status, once prod reconciles — sync only confirms the manifests applied, health tells you whether the rollout is actually working. And because every promotion was nothing more than a Git commit changing one tag, rolling back a bad one is a git revert on that commit: ArgoCD or Flux reconciles the cluster straight back to the previous known-good tag automatically, with no manual kubectl commands and no guessing.

That's the chapter: ArgoCD's Application model, Flux's composable pieces, how to lay a repo out across environments, and a real promotion workflow tying it together with pull requests as the audit trail. Next chapter builds on this with progressive delivery — rolling a promoted change out gradually instead of all at once.
